Thank you very much. Chair, excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honour to speak on behalf of the European Union and its 27 Member States. The European Union and its Member States welcome the renewal and extension of the mandate of the Intergovernmental Working Group on the future strategic framework. We also welcome the work undertaken so far, including the vision and key elements identified for the post-2030 framework. We emphasise that the 16 key elements are interlinked and mutually reinforcing, and we recognize the critical relevance for the future strategic framework. We meet at a time when pressures on land are intensifying in every region. Desertification, land degradation and drought, exacerbated by climate change, are already undermining food security, water availability, biodiversity, resilience and livelihoods. The scale and urgency of these interconnected challenges call on us to act with clarity and ambition. This is why the Convention must equip itself with a robust, forward-looking and effective post-2030 strategic framework. It should help us to respond to emerging challenges, strengthen implementation and reinforce the relevance and impact of the Convention. We encourage strong and continuous involvement of Parties and stakeholders, including through regional consultation with parties and consultations with civil society, the private sector and practitioners. The group should also take into account relevant ongoing and forthcoming inputs, including work on monitoring and indicators, notably on gender and land tenure, lessons from the 2026 reporting process, the recommendation of the midterm evaluation of the 2018 to 2030 strategic framework, and synergies with other multilateral monitoring frameworks. We further call for close coordination and synergies with the development of the post-2030 gender action plan. At the same time, the future's framework should remain flexible enough to reflect different national realities while ensuring that the indicator system is relevant, practical and workable for all parties. We also encourage the group to consider a comprehensive theory of change to help communicate the convention's impact. On ambition, future goals and targets should be science-based, implementation-oriented, and where possible, guided by smart principles. The post-2030 strategic framework should also strengthen proactive drought management while promoting science, gender equality, secure land tenure, and synergies with the Rio Conventions and other relevant global frameworks. The European Union and its Member States remain fully committed to working with all partners towards a strong, credible and effective post-2030 strategic framework. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. We thank you for convening this plenary session and for the opportunity to set our expectations for the future strategic framework of the Convention. We meet at a moment when the challenges this Convention was created to address are growing, not receding. Up to 40% of the world's land is already degraded and this directly affects around half of humanity. The frequency and intensity of droughts have risen by almost 30% since the year of 2000. And current projections indicate that by 2050, three in every four people may be affected by drought. If present trends continue, an additional area almost the size of South America could be degraded within that same period. It's precisely because the stakes are so high that Brazil attaches great importance to the work of the Intergovernmental Working Group of the Future Strategic Framework. Over three in-person sessions and under considerable time constraints, the group delivered a substantive report. We regret that this report could not be fully debated by parties at the session. Its value, however, remains. The group agreed on a shared vision for the post-2030 framework and identified the key elements that such framework should contain. That is a solid foundation. and one that reflects the priorities and perspectives of all regions. At the same time, we recognize that much remains to be done. The elements already identified must now be given more concrete, detailed and operational form, with clear recommendations, sound indicators and a credible approach to the means of implementation. The work cannot be improvised. It requires the continuation of the working group's mandate along the lines defined by decision four of COP16 in Riyadh so that the process keep its transparency, its inclusiveness, and its foundation in consensus. The calendar leaves us little room. The current strategic framework runs only until 2030, and the volume of work still required to shape its successor is considerable. Brazil therefore calls on delegations to support a pragmatic compromise solution that allows the working group to continue its work without interruption. Losing momentum would set back an effort that this convention and the people who depend on healthy land cannot afford to postpone. Mr. co-facilitator, Brazil wishes to be clear on the further point. This conference is convened to address the matters that fall within the mandate of this convention, namely desertification, land degradation, and drought, and those matters alone. This is where our focus should remain. Brazil does not support bringing into this forum questions that are foreign to this convention, and we call against the politicization of environmental issues. Land degradation and drought affect us all with increasing severity and they draw no distinction among nations. Our shared responsibility is to respond to them together and we should not allow considerations extraneous to the common purpose to divert or delay our response. Finally, Brazil remains fully committed to an ambitious and effective post-2030 strategic framework and stands ready to work constructively with all parties to that end. Thank you.

Mr. Chair, on behalf of the Regional Implementation Annex for Central and Eastern Europe, I would like to address an issue for particular and growing importance to our region, drought. Our region includes countries with very diverse climatic, ecological and socioeconomic conditions. Many of our countries have not traditionally been considered highly drought prone, yet increasingly frequent and severe drought episodes are affecting agriculture, water resources, ecosystems, rural livelihoods and economies across Central and Eastern Europe. This experience reinforces a message the Tau region has raised for many years. Drought is a global challenge and should be addressed as such. It does not stop at national borders, nor is it confined to traditionally dry regions. Increasing drought impacts across Europe and other parts of the world demonstrate that preparedness and resilience are challenges for all countries. These trends are already visible across our region. For example, the declining water level of the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland water body, with its accelerating pace, has far-reaching environmental, economic, and social consequences, including contributing to desertification across the region, showing firsthand that the drought is indeed becoming a harsh reality of the region. While in Serbia, around 70% of 10.45 billion euros in weather and climate related losses between 2000 and 2024 was linked to drought and extreme temperatures, including at least 1 billion euros in losses in summer 2024 alone. We recognize the important progress achieved under the convention, including the development of national drought plans, monitoring and early warning tools, knowledge platforms and regional cooperation mechanisms. However, planning alone is not sufficient. The priority now must be implementation. National drought plans need to be translated into concrete actions, investment strategies and projects. Countries need stronger institutional and technical capacities, functioning monitoring and early warning systems, Improved for many countries in our region, particularly those with limited institutional and financial capacities, this remained a significant constraint. Regional cooperation is equally important. Meteorological, agricultural and hydrological drought do not respect borders. Shared water resources, monitoring networks, scientific knowledge and experience provide strong reasons to strengthen regional and sub-regional cooperation as an operational part of drought resilience. Annex V therefore believes that a meaningful outcome on drought is in high demand and recognise the enormous work done to address drought under the UNCCD. We believe it will be a strong basement for the COP18 to make strong commitments to enhance drought resilience and ensure well-being of our communities. We recognize the different views among parties regarding the eventual form of the global drought arrangement, as well as the realities of the current international context. At the same time, these differences should be solved on the basis of consensus. Our region is therefore ready to explore a voluntary country-driven approach that can initiate stronger global cooperation on drought, while allowing that cooperation to evolve over time. The experience of land degradation neutrality demonstrates that voluntary national objectives and targets can create political momentum, improve national coordination, mobilize investment, and progressively strengthen implementation. A similar approach could be explored for drought resilience. Parties could, according to their national circumstances and capacities, voluntarily establish drought resilience objectives, targets or milestones, supported by national drought plans, monitoring and early warning systems, regional cooperation, science, capacity building and access to finance. Such an approach would make maximum use of existing UNCCD institutions, mechanisms and tools, avoid unnecessary additional reporting burdens, and focus on measurable progress and implementation on the ground. Importantly, taking practical action now does not need to prejudge the future. Progress could be reviewed at a future session of the Conference of the Parties, allowing parties to consider whether further measures, institutional arrangements, or strengthened forms of international cooperation are required. We believe that this provides a possible bridge between urgency and political reality. Annex V stands ready for further constructive cooperation with all parties towards a future meaningful decision within the UNCCD that will strengthen proactive drought management and leave the door open for greater ambition in the future. Our objective should be clear, move from plans to implementation. from reaction to preparedness and from fragmented national responses to stronger cooperation on a challenge that is truly global. Thank you, Mr. Chair.
